Renato, the South is down in the third quarter. Before the global review, I need to understand what happened.
Of course. Units in the South declined by twelve percent compared to the second quarter.
Twelve percent is a lot. Is it a real downturn, or something else?
It is not a downturn in the market. The root cause was a stockout in August. A shipment was held at customs for eleven days.
I remember that. So the clinics had no product?
Exactly. Because of the delay, some clinics had nothing for almost three weeks. And part of the July dip is just seasonality.
Did we lose any clients because of it?
Yes, that was the knock-on effect. Due to a price cut from a competitor, two clinics in Porto Alegre switched, and they have not come back yet.
That is the part the global team will ask about. Is the damage temporary?
The stockout was. For the two clinics, we have a recovery plan: joint visits this month, and growth in Curitiba will offset part of the drop.
Good. Start with the number, give one cause, and end with the plan. That is how you say it to the global team.

Every year at least one of my country managers has a bad quarter, and that is normal. What I remember is not the drop. It is the way the manager explains it. The weak explanation starts with excuses, and it takes five minutes to reach a number. The strong one starts with the number. Units fell by twelve percent in the South, full stop. Then it gives me the root cause, only one or two, not a list of ten. Was it a stockout? A competitor? Seasonality? If you give me ten causes, I hear that you do not know the real one. And then, and this is the part most people forget, it tells me what you are doing about it, and when I will see the result. I do not need a perfect recovery plan in the first meeting. I need to see that you understand why it happened, and that you have already started to fix it. A manager who explains a drop well often earns more trust than a manager who never has one.

I run supply planning for Latin America, so when a shipment is late, I am the person who hears about it first. In August, a shipment from our plant in Europe was held at customs for eleven days. Because of that, three distributors in the South ran out of stock, and some clinics had no product for almost three weeks. That was the direct effect. The knock-on effect was worse. Since the clinics could not wait, a few of them tried a competitor, and two of them stayed with it. So a problem that lasted three weeks turned into a problem that could last a year. As a result, we changed two things. First, we now keep six weeks of stock in the South instead of four. Second, when a shipment is late, the commercial team hears about it on the same day, so the sales managers can call the most important clinics before they run out. The stockout was temporary. The lost clinics are not, unless the commercial team wins them back.
